text: MCP follows a client-server architecture with three named roles. The host is the AI application the person actually uses -- Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or an agent you build yourself. It's what coordinates everything else.

A client is a component living inside the host that maintains one dedicated connection to one server and fetches context from it. A server is the program that exposes tools, resources, and prompts to whatever client connects. The detail worth remembering: a host creates one client per server, not one client total.

If VS Code connects to a Sentry server for error tracking and a filesystem server for local files, that's two separate client objects, each with its own connection. Add a third server and you get a third client -- the host coordinates all of them, but every client-server pair runs independently.

'MCP server' doesn't mean local, either. A local server runs on your own machine over stdio, typically serving one client. A remote server, like the official Sentry server, runs on someone else's infrastructure over Streamable HTTP, and can serve many clients at once, the same as any normal web API.

Underneath both, MCP keeps two layers separate: a data layer built on JSON-RPC 2.0 for discovery and the core primitives, and a transport layer -- stdio or Streamable HTTP -- for how those messages actually move. That split is why the same message format works on your laptop or across the internet. Next: what those primitives, tools, resources, and prompts, actually are.
